title: Why Teachers Quit, but I haven't yet
author: Doing Inclusion
summary: A special-education teacher and self-described serial career-changer writes a personal essay on why she has not quit teaching despite nine years of wanting to. She locates teacher attrition not primarily in workload or pay but in feeling professionally invisible: leadership that doesn't recognize pre-teaching experience, doesn't know staff as whole people, and doesn't check in during personal crises. The piece pivots on two recent moments of feeling seen (a comment from linguist Lyn Stone, and camaraderie at ResearchEd Canberra) that lead her to a reframing of what it means to be called "inspiring." She lands on a somewhat unconventional etymological insight: that to inspire literally means to cause someone to breathe in, and that being an inspiration to others is really about making them pause and reflect, not about her own specialness. The essay closes as a direct address to struggling teachers, urging them to seek out professional communities (Think Forward Educators, ResearchEd) rather than leave the profession. It reads as archivable for the teaching-profession/identity/burnout angle central to Education - Practice & Culture, with direct implications for how school leaders should treat staff.
points: Frames teacher attrition as fundamentally about feeling unseen and unacknowledged by school leadership, not simply about workload or pay.
Draws on her own career-changer, AuDHD-influenced restlessness (jobs across 20 of 26 letters of the alphabet) to explain both her flight risk and what has kept her in teaching for nine years.
Argues school leaders should personally know one fact about every staff member and check in during personal crises, framing that as a baseline of leadership rather than an extra.

Traces a personal turning point in which external validation (a comment from linguist Lyn Stone, camaraderie at ResearchEd Canberra) leads to a reframing that self-recognition, not others' recognition, is what was actually missing.
Closes with a direct appeal to teachers considering quitting to seek out professional communities such as Think Forward Educators and ResearchEd rather than leave the profession.
quotes: This is why teachers leave. We often don't feel seen or acknowledged. We rarely have a cheer squad in our schools celebrating our sometimes extraordinary wins.
Don't make teachers feel like they have to fight to get good educational outcomes for kids - that should be the bread and butter of teaching.
If you're a school leader and you don't know one personal fact about every person in your school, I challenge you to get out there walking around and speaking to your staff.

My struggle has been that I feel invisible as a whole person. I don't feel like my school leadership see me or appreciate any of the results I've achieved, or just how much I can offer because I'm just a teacher.
This morning I woke up and realised, for possibly the second time in my life, that it is not others who don't see me that bothers me, it is that I don't see myself.
When you challenge people to be better and help them believe they can, it is inspiring. When you make people stop and think that there could be another way, it is inspiring.
So, if you're a teacher going through it and feeling all the thoughts of quitting, please take heart because you can find your tribe.
